title: Gordon Bell Prize Goes to Chinese Team for Exascale FeMoco Solution - HPCwire
html:
This year’s prestigious ACM Gordon Bell Prize has gone to a 10 member Chinese team for their outstanding work in quantum chemistry. The winners were announced at SC26. Their project named Closing the FeMo-Cofactor “Quantum-Advantage” Gap with Exascale Supercomputers used traditional supercomputers to take on a problem that many believe quantum computers will be better at solving.

Researchers have been trying to figure out where classical computing reaches its limits for years. They have also been interested in where quantum computers might have an advantage. However, those limits keep changing as supercomputers and the software running on them improve. This year’s winning team has shown that there may still be more room for classical machines to improve – at least more than what was thought previously.

ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) says the team is recognized for developing the first “exascale” classical solution to the FeMoco CAS problem.

The research focuses on FeMoco, an active site inside the enzyme nitrogenase. It helps certain organisms turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. The problem is figuring out how its electrons behave. That would provide a better understanding of how it works and then use that for different applications such finding cheaper ways to make fertilizer for food supply.

However, there are so many possible ways they can interact. Even the largest supercomputers have trouble calculating them all. To make matters more complex, the more electrons researchers try to account for, the harder the job gets.

LineShine from China is number 1 on the TOP500 list

So where does quantum computing come into the picture? FeMoco has been used for years as an example of a calculation that quantum computers could eventually do much faster. However, that depends on how much progress classical computers make in the meantime.

There’s a limit to what we can take from this result. The Chinese team needed a huge amount of computing power to get the job done, so it’s not as though FeMoco has suddenly become easy to simulate. And quantum computers may still turn out to be much better at this kind of work. We just don’t know yet.

Quantum computers are getting better, but traditional supercomputers are improving too. So it’s still hard to say when quantum computers will have a clear advantage.

The other two Gordon Bell finalists worked on very different problems. One team, from Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM, used quantum computers alongside CPUs and GPUs to simulate a protein containing 12,635 atoms. It was the largest protein known to have been simulated using quantum computers, with the researchers using up to 94 qubits.

The Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM researchers had to get quantum processors, CPUs, and GPUs working together. That isn’t always easy when data needs to move between different systems. The team found ways to reduce the manual work involved, which also meant fewer chances of errors. The quantum computer handled part of the calculation, while the other processors did the rest.

The third finalist was working on fusion energy. The researchers wanted to see how liquid metal behaves inside a part of a fusion reactor called a breeding blanket. This component helps produce tritium, one of the fuels needed for fusion.

They used Aurora at Argonne and Frontier at Oak Ridge to run their simulations. The team ran an open-source code called NekRS on more than 9,000 nodes on each machine. That’s nearly the full capacity of both supercomputers.

Aurora Supercomputer at Argonne Labs (Credit: Argonne/ALCF)

Aurora and Frontier use different GPU hardware, so running the same code on both at that scale wasn’t easy. It’s something that matters for HPC researchers, who often have to make changes to their software when moving from one machine to another.

There was also a separate Gordon Bell Prize for Climate Modelling. This went to a 13-member team led by researchers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

The team used AI to improve weather and climate forecasting. Weather models need information from satellites, weather stations, and other sources to make predictions. Scientists have to bring all this information together and feed it into their models, a process called data assimilation.

There’s a lot of data involved, and processing it takes considerable computing power. The researchers developed an AI method to make the process faster and less demanding. Their work could help improve forecasts of hurricanes and other extreme weather.

The Gordon Bell Prize has recognized advances in parallel computing since 1987. Last year’s main winner was a real-time tsunami early-warning digital twin developed by researchers from UT Austin, Lawrence Livermore, and Scripps.

Looking at this year’s projects, there’s quite a range of work being done. Some researchers are pushing the limits of what computers can calculate, while others are trying to make existing methods work better. And as these machines get more powerful, figuring out how to use them well remains a big part of the challenge.
